options.a: Side-to-side sloshing that occurs only in fully loaded tanks
options.b: Pressure buildup in the tank as the product heats and expands
options.c: Vapor movement through the vents during loading and unloading
options.d: Forward and back movement of liquid that can push the vehicle

distractorExplanations.a: Surge is mainly forward-and-back wave motion and is worst in partially filled tanks; a full tank leaves little room for liquid to move.
distractorExplanations.b: Heat-driven expansion is the reason outage is left in the tank; it is a volume issue, not the wave motion that pushes the truck.
distractorExplanations.c: Vapor flow through vents is a loading and vapor-control issue; surge is the liquid itself moving and shoving the vehicle.

options.a: Filled to capacity with no free surface
options.b: Partially filled so liquid can move freely
options.c: Divided by baffles into smaller compartments
options.d: Nearly empty with only vapor left inside

distractorExplanations.a: A tank filled to capacity has almost no free surface, so liquid cannot build momentum; partial loads surge far more.
distractorExplanations.c: Baffles slow forward-and-back flow, so a baffled tank surges less than a partially filled smooth-bore tank.
distractorExplanations.d: With only vapor inside there is no liquid mass to surge; the danger comes from a partial liquid load moving freely.

options.a: Stop side-to-side surge as well as forward surge
options.b: Separate different products into sealed compartments
options.c: Allow liquid to expand without overfilling the tank
options.d: Slow liquid surge through bulkheads with openings

distractorExplanations.a: Baffles slow forward-and-back surge, but the CDL manual warns that side-to-side surge still occurs and can cause rollover.
distractorExplanations.b: Solid bulkheads divide a tank into sealed compartments; baffles have openings and exist to slow surge, not separate products.
distractorExplanations.c: Room for expansion is provided by outage (leaving empty space), not by baffles inside the tank.

options.a: Less care because smooth bores haul lighter food loads
options.b: Faster cornering since surge settles quickly
options.c: Smoother control because surge can be greater
options.d: The same following distance as a baffled tank of equal size

distractorExplanations.a: Smooth-bore tanks often carry food products such as milk, but with nothing to slow the liquid the forward-and-back surge is stronger, so more care is needed.
distractorExplanations.b: With no baffles, surge in a smooth-bore tank is stronger and lasts longer; cornering speed should be lower, not higher.
distractorExplanations.d: An unbaffled tank has stronger surge than a baffled one, so it needs more space and smoother braking, not the same distance.

options.a: Surge forward, then surge back as the vehicle settles
options.b: Move mostly side to side rather than forward and back
options.c: Stay in place if the tank has baffles installed
options.d: Shorten stopping distance by adding weight to the drive axles

distractorExplanations.b: In a hard stop the liquid surges forward and then back along the length of the tank; side-to-side surge is the curve hazard.
distractorExplanations.c: Baffles slow surge but do not stop the liquid from moving; a baffled tank still surges in a hard stop.
distractorExplanations.d: Forward surge pushes the truck ahead after braking starts, which lengthens the stop rather than shortening it.

options.a: Lower rollover risk since liquid keeps the center of gravity low
options.b: Be safe at the posted advisory curve speed
options.c: Raise rollover risk as liquid surges sideways
options.d: Push the trailer forward rather than toward the outside

distractorExplanations.a: A tank vehicle has a high center of gravity, and liquid shifting sideways in a curve raises rollover risk rather than lowering it.
distractorExplanations.b: The CDL manual warns that tankers can roll over at the posted curve speed; take curves well below the advisory speed.
distractorExplanations.d: In a curve the liquid surges toward the outside of the turn, adding sideways force; forward push is the braking hazard.

options.a: Reduce surge forces on the vehicle
options.b: Eliminate side-to-side surge in curves
options.c: Reduce tire wear on drive axles
options.d: Prevent product expansion in the tank

distractorExplanations.b: Smooth starts and stops lessen forward-and-back surge; side-to-side surge in curves is controlled by lower speed, and it is not eliminated.
distractorExplanations.c: Tire wear is a side benefit at most; the reason the manual stresses smooth control is to limit surge forces on the vehicle.
distractorExplanations.d: Product expansion depends on temperature and is managed by outage, not by how smoothly the driver starts and stops.

options.a: Control surge and add tank structure
options.b: Let liquid flow freely end to end
options.c: Provide the outage space the product needs
options.d: Replace the need to check weight distribution

distractorExplanations.b: Solid bulkheads stop liquid from flowing between compartments; letting it flow freely end to end is what a smooth-bore tank does.
distractorExplanations.c: Outage is the empty space left in each compartment for expansion; bulkheads are dividing walls, not expansion room.
distractorExplanations.d: The CDL manual says to check weight distribution when loading or unloading bulkhead compartments so front or rear axles are not overloaded.

options.a: The amount of product unloaded at delivery
options.b: Liquid remaining after the tank is unloaded
options.c: Empty space left for product expansion
options.d: Vapor pressure inside the tank

distractorExplanations.a: Outage is the space deliberately left unfilled for expansion, not the volume delivered to the customer.
distractorExplanations.b: Liquid left in the tank after unloading is the residue or heel; outage is the empty space left when loading.
distractorExplanations.d: Vapor pressure is a property of the product; outage is the physical empty space allowed so the liquid can expand.

options.a: Shorten stopping distance by loading the axles
options.b: Affect empty tanks more than partial loads
options.c: Extend stopping distance and upset control
options.d: Be cancelled by ABS on dry pavement

distractorExplanations.a: Forward surge pushes the truck ahead after the brakes are applied, so the stop gets longer, not shorter.
distractorExplanations.b: An empty tank has no liquid to surge; surge is a partial-load problem, even though empty trucks need more distance for traction reasons.
distractorExplanations.d: ABS prevents wheel lockup but cannot stop the liquid's momentum; surge still pushes the truck and upsets control.

options.a: Only the volume of outage required
options.b: Handling, braking demand, and stability
options.c: The placard color required on the tank
options.d: Fuel economy but not braking or rollover risk

distractorExplanations.a: Outage depends on how much the product expands with heat; density mainly limits how much can be loaded before hitting weight limits.
distractorExplanations.c: Placards are set by the hazard class of the material, not by its density or weight.
distractorExplanations.d: Heavier, denser loads raise braking demand and change stability, so density matters for braking and rollover, not just fuel use.

options.a: Fill level affects weight but not surge behavior
options.b: Empty tanks surge the most of any fill level
options.c: Partial loads often surge more than full loads
options.d: Baffled tanks can be filled to any level safely

distractorExplanations.a: Fill level directly controls surge: a partially filled tank leaves room for the liquid to build momentum and push the truck.
distractorExplanations.b: An empty tank has no liquid to surge; partially filled tanks surge the most.
distractorExplanations.d: Baffles slow surge but do not remove outage limits or side-to-side surge, so fill level still has to be managed.

options.a: End as soon as the wheels stop, so brakes can be released
options.b: Rock the vehicle — stay braked and secured until settled
options.c: Signal a baffle failure that needs immediate unloading
options.d: Push the truck forward only if the tank is full

distractorExplanations.a: Liquid keeps moving after the wheels stop and can push the truck; releasing the brakes too soon lets it roll.
distractorExplanations.c: Some residual surge is normal after a hard stop, even with intact baffles; it does not by itself mean the baffles failed.
distractorExplanations.d: A full tank has little room for surge; residual push is strongest with a partial load.

options.a: Firm braking early so the surge hits before the stop
options.b: Smooth control and appropriate speed for conditions
options.c: Posted ramp speeds, since they are set for loaded trucks
options.d: Coasting in neutral downhill to avoid brake surges

distractorExplanations.a: Hard or early braking creates surge rather than managing it; steady, smooth brake pressure keeps surge forces low.
distractorExplanations.c: Posted ramp and curve speeds are set for cars; the CDL manual says tankers can roll over at those speeds.
distractorExplanations.d: Coasting in neutral removes engine braking and is unsafe and illegal in many states; gear selection plus smooth braking controls downhill speed.

options.a: The tank's full liquid volume capacity
options.b: The gross limit alone, ignoring axle weights
options.c: The tank's volume minus a fixed 1% outage
options.d: Legal and manufacturer weight ratings

distractorExplanations.a: Dense liquids can reach legal weight limits long before the tank is full, so volume capacity is not the overload limit.
distractorExplanations.b: Legal limits include individual axle weights as well as gross weight; meeting gross weight alone can still overload an axle.
distractorExplanations.c: Outage varies with how much the product expands, and weight ratings still apply; there is no fixed 1% rule that sets the limit.

options.a: Tire wear but no handling change
options.b: Lean and higher rollover risk
options.c: Forward-and-back surge
options.d: Problems only on unbaffled tanks

distractorExplanations.a: Weight shifted to one side makes the tanker lean and lowers the speed at which it can roll over, so handling does change.
distractorExplanations.c: Forward-and-back surge comes from braking and acceleration; uneven side-to-side loading causes lean and rollover risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Side-to-side imbalance raises rollover risk on any tank; baffles only slow forward-and-back surge.

options.a: Product contamination but not leaks
options.b: Leaks, spills, and pressure problems
options.c: Loss of outage space during loading
options.d: Baffle damage from vapor surge

distractorExplanations.a: Loose hatches and domes let product leak or spill and allow pressure to escape; contamination is not the main hazard.
distractorExplanations.c: Outage is set by how full the tank is filled, not by whether the dome cover is secured.
distractorExplanations.d: Baffles are internal walls that slow liquid surge; an unsecured dome causes leaks and pressure loss, not baffle damage.

options.a: The tank specification plate alone
options.b: Shipping papers, placards, and SDS as applicable
options.c: The previous load listed in the logbook
options.d: The terminal operator's verbal description at loading

distractorExplanations.a: The specification plate describes the tank's design and test data, not the hazards of the product currently loaded.
distractorExplanations.c: The previous load tells you nothing reliable about the current product; its hazards come from current papers and placards.
distractorExplanations.d: A verbal description is not a hazard communication document; drivers rely on shipping papers, placards, and SDS.

options.a: Keeping the engine in gear instead of setting brakes
options.b: Controlling the vehicle and preventing rollaway
options.c: Setting only the trailer hand valve as a parking brake
options.d: Relying on transmission park alone

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving the truck in gear does not replace the parking brakes; on a grade the brakes must be set to prevent rollaway.
distractorExplanations.c: The trailer hand valve must not be used for parking because air can leak off and release the trailer brakes.
distractorExplanations.d: Not the best answer: Relying on transmission park alone always.

options.a: Expansion spills and pressure problems
options.b: More surge than a partially filled tank
options.c: Problems only when the product is cold
options.d: Vapor loss, but no liquid spills

distractorExplanations.b: An overfilled tank has little free surface, so surge is not the risk; the risk is the product expanding with no outage.
distractorExplanations.c: A cold product overfilled at loading will expand as it warms in transit, which is exactly when spills and pressure problems occur.
distractorExplanations.d: Without outage, expanding liquid can push out through vents and fittings, so liquid spills are a real risk.

options.a: Left until the next annual tank test if there is no leak
options.b: Inspected and reported because it affects surge control
options.c: Repaired by the driver at the next fuel stop
options.d: Noted only if the tank is hauling hazmat

distractorExplanations.a: Damaged baffles change surge control right away, so the defect must be reported now, not left for a periodic test.
distractorExplanations.c: Internal baffle repairs need a qualified repair facility; the driver's job is to inspect and report the defect.
distractorExplanations.d: Baffles control surge for any liquid load, so damage must be reported whether or not the cargo is hazardous.

options.a: Rated for pressure even if not product-compatible
options.b: Hand-tightened and checked after unloading begins
options.c: Connected after the valves are opened
options.d: Correct, tight, and compatible with the product

distractorExplanations.a: A hose rated for pressure but not compatible with the product can degrade or fail; it must match the product too.
distractorExplanations.b: Connections must be checked tight before product starts flowing; checking after unloading begins risks a spill.
distractorExplanations.c: Hoses are connected and checked before valves are opened; opening valves first would release product.

options.a: Bonding and grounding procedures as required
options.b: Grounding after product transfer is complete
options.c: A drag chain in place of bonding cables
options.d: Splash filling from the top to speed loading

distractorExplanations.b: Bonding and grounding must be connected before transfer starts and stay connected until it ends, not added afterward.
distractorExplanations.c: A drag chain is not a substitute for the bonding and grounding connections required during flammable transfers.
distractorExplanations.d: Splash filling increases static charge buildup; it raises the ignition risk instead of controlling it.

options.a: Only the tire pressures and lights
options.b: Papers and placards, leaving leak and valve checks for later
options.c: Securements, leaks, papers, placards, and weights
options.d: Leaks at the next scheduled stop instead

distractorExplanations.a: Tires and lights matter, but after loading the driver must also recheck securements, leaks, papers, placards, and weights.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaks, valves, and closures must be checked before departure, not just the paperwork and placards.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaks must be found before leaving the loading site; waiting until the next stop risks a release on the road.

options.a: The same handling as ambient fuel loads
options.b: Venting to atmosphere to cool the load faster
options.c: Water cooling of the shell before unloading
options.d: Special temperature and handling procedures

distractorExplanations.a: Heated products such as asphalt carry burn and pressure hazards that ambient fuel loads do not, so handling differs.
distractorExplanations.b: Venting product to atmosphere to cool it is a release, not an approved handling step for heated cargo.
distractorExplanations.c: Cooling the shell with water is not an approved step; heated cargo follows the shipper's temperature and handling procedures.

options.a: Only the gross weight, not axle limits
options.b: Fuel economy but not steering or braking
options.c: Steering, braking, and axle limit compliance
options.d: Tire wear, with no effect on axle limits

distractorExplanations.a: Weight distribution decides how much each axle carries, so it governs axle-limit compliance as well as gross weight.
distractorExplanations.b: Too much weight on the front or rear changes steering response and braking, not just fuel economy.
distractorExplanations.d: Poor distribution can overload one axle beyond its legal limit even when the gross weight is legal.

options.a: At the posted advisory speed, since it is set for tank vehicles
options.b: With hard braking in the curve to settle the surge
options.c: At normal speed when the tank is baffled
options.d: Slower than with dry freight because of surge and high CG

distractorExplanations.a: Posted curve speeds are set for cars; the CDL manual says tankers can roll over at the posted speed.
distractorExplanations.b: Braking hard inside the curve adds surge and shifts weight while the tanker is already leaning; slow down before the curve.
distractorExplanations.c: Baffles slow only forward-and-back surge; side-to-side surge and the high center of gravity still demand lower curve speed.

options.a: Reduced, since a loaded tank stops shorter
options.b: The same as for a dry van of equal weight
options.c: Increased for longer stopping dynamics
options.d: Unchanged when the truck has ABS

distractorExplanations.a: A loaded tank does not stop shorter; surge can push the truck after braking starts, so more space is needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Liquid surge makes a tanker's stop less predictable than a dry van of the same weight, so it needs extra space.
distractorExplanations.d: ABS prevents wheel lockup but does not cancel surge or shorten stopping distance, so following distance still increases.

options.a: Neutral coasting with light braking
options.b: Proper gearing and controlled braking
options.c: Steady light braking from top to bottom
options.d: Downshifting once speed starts to build

distractorExplanations.a: Coasting in neutral removes engine braking and makes brakes overheat; the right gear must be engaged before the grade.
distractorExplanations.c: Constant light pressure is riding the brakes, which overheats them and causes fade on long grades.
distractorExplanations.d: The gear must be chosen before starting down; downshifting after speed builds may be impossible or overheat the brakes.

options.a: Better traction from more weight pressing on the tires
options.b: Greater rollover risk in turns and lane changes
options.c: Lower rollover risk than a loaded dry van
options.d: Rollover risk only on unbaffled tanks

distractorExplanations.a: A high center of gravity relates to rollover, not traction; most of the weight is carried high above the road.
distractorExplanations.c: Tankers usually carry their weight higher than dry vans, so rollover risk is greater, not lower.
distractorExplanations.d: High center of gravity raises rollover risk on any tank vehicle; baffles only slow forward-and-back surge.

options.a: Quick, to limit time spent straddling lanes
options.b: Signaled only after starting the move
options.c: Made while braking to settle the load
options.d: Gradual with mirror checks and space

distractorExplanations.a: Quick lane changes swing a high-CG tanker and start side surge; lane changes should be gradual.
distractorExplanations.b: Signal before moving so traffic can react; signaling after the move starts gives others no warning.
distractorExplanations.c: Braking during a lane change combines forward and side surge; brake before or after the move, not during it.

options.a: Even more speed reduction and smoothness
options.b: The same speed, relying on ABS for control
options.c: Higher speed to keep momentum on grades
options.d: Hard braking to settle the liquid load

distractorExplanations.b: ABS helps keep steering control but does not shorten stops or stop surge, so speed must still come down on slick roads.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher speed on slippery roads raises skid and surge risk; liquid cargo calls for lower speed and smooth control.
distractorExplanations.d: Hard braking on a slick surface invites skids and starts surge; smooth, gentle braking is required.

options.a: Pick a lower gear only after speed builds on the grade
options.b: Check brakes and choose a safe speed/gear early
options.c: Set cruise control to hold a steady speed
options.d: Switch off the retarder on dry pavement

distractorExplanations.a: The right gear must be selected before starting downhill; trying to downshift after speed builds can fail.
distractorExplanations.c: Cruise control does not provide braking on a downgrade; the driver must choose a low gear and control speed.
distractorExplanations.d: A retarder helps control speed on dry downgrades; it is turned off on slippery roads, not on dry pavement.

options.a: Shorten stops by loading the drive axles
options.b: Pull the truck backward as you brake
options.c: Add push after you start braking
options.d: Matter mainly when the tank is empty

distractorExplanations.a: Forward surge pushes the truck ahead after braking begins, which lengthens the stop rather than shortening it.
distractorExplanations.b: When you brake, the liquid first surges forward and pushes the truck ahead; the backward surge comes after the stop.
distractorExplanations.d: An empty tank has no liquid to surge; surge is a partial-load hazard.

options.a: Demand extra caution and smooth control
options.b: Are best crossed with a gear change on the tracks
options.c: Can be crossed quickly to limit time on tracks
options.d: Are exempt from stopping rules

distractorExplanations.b: Drivers must not shift gears while crossing tracks; choose a gear that will carry the truck all the way across before starting.
distractorExplanations.c: Speeding across tracks starts surge and risks loss of control; tankers need caution and smooth, steady speed.
distractorExplanations.d: Not the best answer: Are exempt from stopping rules always.

options.a: Release the brakes at once to ride out the push
options.b: Keep control; do not release chaotically
options.c: Pump the brakes hard until the surge stops
options.d: Shift to neutral so the drivetrain absorbs it

distractorExplanations.a: Releasing the brakes when surge pushes lets the truck roll forward; the manual says keep steady brake pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: Hard pumping creates repeated surges; steady controlled pressure is what keeps the truck stable.
distractorExplanations.d: Shifting to neutral removes engine braking and control; it does not absorb surge forces.

options.a: Posted advisory speeds plus tanker dynamics
options.b: Posted advisory speeds, which suit any truck
options.c: The same speed used with dry freight
options.d: The speed of surrounding truck traffic

distractorExplanations.b: Advisory ramp speeds are set for cars; tankers can roll over at those speeds and must go slower.
distractorExplanations.c: Liquid surge and a high center of gravity mean a tanker needs lower ramp speeds than dry freight.
distractorExplanations.d: Other trucks may be empty or carrying dry freight; a tanker's ramp speed must reflect its own load dynamics.

options.a: Greater surge because liquid cools at night
options.b: Stricter hours-of-service rules that apply only at night
options.c: Reduced visibility of hazards and soft shoulders
options.d: Glare from placards reflecting headlights

distractorExplanations.a: Night temperature does not meaningfully change surge; the night risk is reduced visibility of hazards and road edges.
distractorExplanations.b: Hours-of-service limits are not stricter at night; the added risk is seeing hazards and soft shoulders in the dark.
distractorExplanations.d: Reflective placards are not a recognized night hazard; the risk is not seeing hazards and soft shoulders in time.

options.a: Combined with high CG and liquid movement
options.b: The tank is filled with no outage left
options.c: You reduce speed below the posted limit
options.d: The tank has baffles installed

distractorExplanations.b: A tank with no outage is an expansion and spill problem; wind raises rollover risk mainly through high CG and sideways liquid movement.
distractorExplanations.c: Slowing down lowers wind-related rollover risk; it does not make the tanker less stable.
distractorExplanations.d: Baffles reduce forward-and-back surge; they do not make a tank more vulnerable to crosswinds.

options.a: Phone use only at speeds under 20 mph
options.b: Hands-free calling, which removes the distraction risk
options.c: Attention mainly in curves and on ramps
options.d: Continuous attention to space and feel of the load

distractorExplanations.a: CMV drivers may not use a hand-held phone while driving at any speed; there is no low-speed exception.
distractorExplanations.b: Hands-free calls still take mental attention; they are legal but do not remove distraction risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Surge and stopping hazards occur on straight roads too; tankers need continuous attention, not only in curves.

options.a: Keep driving to the terminal to unload
options.b: Stop at the nearest fuel stop for help
options.c: Stop and open the dome to check the level
options.d: Move to a safe location, secure the scene

distractorExplanations.a: Driving on with a leak spreads product along the road; the driver must stop in a safe location right away.
distractorExplanations.b: A fuel stop has people and ignition sources; a leaking tanker should stop away from people and buildings.
distractorExplanations.c: Opening the dome can release vapors and expose the driver; follow emergency procedures instead of inspecting the tank top.

options.a: Fight the fire with nearby water first, then call for help
options.b: Stay beside the tank to guide responders in
options.c: Drive to a service shop so mechanics can check it
options.d: Evacuate to a safe distance and call emergency services

distractorExplanations.a: Water can spread some flammable liquid fires, and drivers should call for help first instead of fighting a cargo fire.
distractorExplanations.b: Staying beside a tank with flammable cargo exposes the driver to fire or explosion; move to a safe distance.
distractorExplanations.c: Driving a tanker at fire risk to a shop carries the hazard into populated areas; stop, evacuate, and call.

options.a: Level secure parking with brakes set
options.b: A soft shoulder clear of traffic lanes
options.c: Trailer hand valve set as the parking brake
options.d: Leaving it in gear on a grade without brakes

distractorExplanations.b: A soft shoulder may not support a loaded tanker and can lead to a rollover; park on firm, level ground.
distractorExplanations.c: The trailer hand valve must not be used for parking; air can bleed off and release the brakes.
distractorExplanations.d: Being in gear does not replace the parking brakes, especially on a grade with a heavy liquid load.

options.a: Speed up slightly to restore steering feel
options.b: Brake hard at once to settle the load
options.c: Reduce speed smoothly and seek a safe stop to inspect
options.d: Continue to the terminal and report the problem to the shop there

distractorExplanations.a: Speeding up with unstable steering makes control worse; slow down smoothly and stop to inspect.
distractorExplanations.b: Hard braking with unstable steering can start surge or a skid; reduce speed smoothly.
distractorExplanations.d: A sudden steering change can mean a tire or suspension failure; stop safely and inspect instead of driving on.

options.a: Shipping papers and required emergency documents
options.b: The tank specification plate on the shell
options.c: The placard alone, without the papers
options.d: The driver's annual vehicle inspection report in the cab

distractorExplanations.b: The specification plate describes the tank's construction and tests, not emergency response details for the product.
distractorExplanations.c: Placards show hazard class but not the full emergency response details; those come with the shipping papers.
distractorExplanations.d: The annual inspection report covers the vehicle's condition, not emergency response for the cargo.

options.a: Call trained responders and give them the product details
options.b: Secure ignition sources from a safe position
options.c: Follow the emergency plan on the shipping papers
options.d: Walk into vapors without proper protection and training

distractorExplanations.a: Calling responders with the product details is a required step after a release, so it is not something to avoid.
distractorExplanations.c: Following the emergency response information that travels with the papers is the correct action, not a prohibited one.
distractorExplanations.b: Not the best answer: Secure ignition sources from a safe position.

options.a: They burn out quickly with no reignition
options.b: They mainly risk damage to the brake lines
options.c: They are unrelated to cargo risk
options.d: Heat can threaten the cargo and tank integrity

distractorExplanations.a: Tire fires can reignite after they seem out, and their heat can reach the tank; they are not quick, harmless fires.
distractorExplanations.b: Brake-line damage is possible, but the serious danger is heat reaching the tank and the cargo.
distractorExplanations.c: Not the best answer: They are unrelated to cargo risk.

options.a: Leave papers in the cab and move downhill
options.b: Shelter in a low ditch close to the vehicle until help comes
options.c: Take shipping papers if safe and move upwind/uphill
options.d: Stay with the vehicle to keep others away

distractorExplanations.a: Responders need the shipping papers, and vapors and liquids flow downhill; take papers if safe and go uphill.
distractorExplanations.b: Low ground near the vehicle collects heavier-than-air vapors and spilled liquid; move upwind and uphill instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Staying with a vehicle that must be abandoned exposes the driver; warn others from a safe distance.

options.a: Righting the tank quickly to stop the leak
options.b: Offloading product into nearby containers
options.c: Life safety, scene control, and proper notifications
options.d: Photographing the damage for insurance before calling for help

distractorExplanations.a: Righting a rolled tanker needs trained crews and equipment; the driver's priorities are life safety and notifications.
distractorExplanations.b: Transferring product needs trained responders and proper equipment; improvised containers can worsen the release.
distractorExplanations.d: Photos come after life safety; delaying the call slows emergency response to the rollover.

options.a: Keep driving and check it at the next stop
options.b: Close the vents and run recirculated air
options.c: Treat as hazardous — ventilate, stop safely
options.d: Assume it is engine exhaust and continue

distractorExplanations.a: An unknown product odor in the cab may mean a leak; stop safely now rather than waiting until the next stop.
distractorExplanations.b: Closing vents traps vapors in the cab; the driver should ventilate and stop safely.
distractorExplanations.d: Assuming the odor is exhaust ignores a possible cargo leak; treat unknown odors as hazardous.

options.a: Tape it and continue slowly
options.b: Continue if it is not leaking yet
options.c: Reseat it with a hammer and go on
options.d: Do not continue as if normal

distractorExplanations.a: Tape is not an approved valve repair; a damaged valve must be handled under out-of-service and repair rules.
distractorExplanations.b: A damaged valve can fail without warning; no visible leak does not make it safe to continue.
distractorExplanations.c: Striking a valve can cause sparks or further damage; valve repairs need a qualified repair facility.

options.a: The carrier name, your truck number, and your expected ETA
options.b: The placard color as seen from the cab
options.c: Product identity, quantity, and hazards from papers
options.d: Your estimate of the cause of the leak

distractorExplanations.a: Carrier, truck, and ETA details help, but responders first need the product identity, quantity, and hazards from the papers.
distractorExplanations.b: Placard color alone does not identify the product or quantity; give responders the details on the shipping papers.
distractorExplanations.d: A guess about the cause does not tell responders what they face; product identity, quantity, and hazards do.

options.a: Proper loading, inspection, speed management
options.b: Baffles and ABS doing the surge control work
options.c: Posted speeds plus a post-trip check only
options.d: Full loads so there is no room for surge

distractorExplanations.b: Baffles and ABS help but do not replace driver speed management and smooth control in preventing emergencies.
distractorExplanations.c: Posted speeds can be too fast for tankers, and a pre-trip inspection is needed before driving, not just a post-trip check.
distractorExplanations.d: Tanks must leave outage for expansion, so filling to the top to avoid surge creates spill and pressure problems.
